title: 2 Kings 16:1–9
context: Ahaz begins to reign in Judah and does not do what is right like David. He walks in the way of Israel's kings, even making his son pass through the fire, and worships at the high places. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem, Ahaz sends temple and palace treasure to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria, calling himself his servant and son. Assyria takes Damascus and kills Rezin. Isaiah 7 records the prophet's call to Ahaz to trust the LORD in this same crisis.

verses.text: In the seventeenth year of Pekah the son of Remaliah, Ahaz the son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz begins to reign in the seventeenth year of Pekah. Arminian readers note that he comes to the throne amid the Syrian and Israelite threat already begun under Jotham (15:37).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the dating connects Ahaz's reign with Israel's final kings. The two kingdoms' fates are intertwined as Assyria's power grows.

verses.text: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He didn’t do that which was right in the LORD his God’s eyes, like David his father.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz is twenty and reigns sixteen years, but "didn't do that which was right" like David. Arminian readers note the clear verdict on a king who chose not to follow the faithfulness of his father and grandfather.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the comparison is to David, the standard for Judah's kings. Ahaz's failure is measured against the covenant promises given to David's line.

verses.text: But he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and even made his son to pass through the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom the LORD cast out from before the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: He walks in the way of Israel's kings and "even made his son to pass through the fire." Arminian readers name this plainly as child sacrifice (compare 2 Chronicles 28:3), an abomination God forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers grieve with the text: God says of such sacrifice, "which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind" (Jeremiah 7:31). A son of David has adopted the practices of the nations God cast out.

verses.text: He sacrificed and burned incense in the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
verses.arminianNotes: He sacrifices and burns incense at the high places and "under every green tree." Arminian readers see a king freely embracing the worship practices that God had commanded Israel to abolish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language echoes the description of Judah under Rehoboam. Ahaz takes Judah further into the idolatry that had brought judgment on Israel.

verses.text: Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem to wage war. They besieged Ahaz, but could not overcome him.
verses.arminianNotes: Rezin and Pekah besiege Jerusalem but cannot overcome Ahaz. Arminian readers note that Isaiah 7:4 records God's word to Ahaz in this crisis: "Be careful, and keep calm. Don't be afraid."
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Isaiah 7:1 says the attackers "could not prevail against it." God protects Jerusalem for David's sake, even under an unfaithful king.

verses.text: At that time Rezin king of Syria recovered Elath to Syria, and drove the Jews from Elath; and the Syrians came to Elath, and live there to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Rezin recovers Elath for Syria and drives out the Jews. Arminian readers note the territorial loss as a consequence of Judah's weakness during Ahaz's reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the loss of Elath, Judah's port on the Red Sea, shows the shrinking of Judah's power. The kingdom is diminished as its king turns from God.

verses.text: So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria, saying, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria and out of the hand of the king of Israel, who rise up against me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz sends to Tiglath-pileser: "I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me." Arminian readers see a king choosing to trust Assyria rather than God, despite Isaiah's call: "If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established" (Isaiah 7:9).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ahaz offers Assyria the language of covenant loyalty that belonged to the LORD. Isaiah 8:6–7 warns that the king of Assyria will become a flood over the land.

verses.text: Ahaz took the silver and gold that was found in the LORD’s house, and in the treasures of the king’s house, and sent it for a present to the king of Assyria.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahaz sends silver and gold from the temple and palace to Assyria. Arminian readers note that he spends the treasures of God's house to buy protection from a foreign king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the tragic exchange: the treasures dedicated to the LORD are given to secure a human alliance. The temple's wealth becomes tribute to a pagan empire.

verses.text: The king of Assyria listened to him; and the king of Assyria went up against Damascus and took it, and carried its people captive to Kir, and killed Rezin.
verses.arminianNotes: Assyria takes Damascus, deports its people to Kir, and kills Rezin. Arminian readers note that Ahaz's plan seems to succeed, though at the cost of making Judah a vassal of Assyria.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God had already said the threat from Rezin would not stand (Isaiah 7). Ahaz's alliance brings short-term relief but long-term subjection.
